reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / ATS-IDSA NTM guidance
clinicalPearls: A slow-growing photochromogenic mycobacterium that grows best at cooler temperatures (around 30 degrees Celsius), which explains its predilection for the skin of the cooler distal extremities
Classically acquired from aquaria, fish handling, and fresh or salt water, giving rise to the terms fish-tank and swimming-pool granuloma; a careful exposure history is the key to suspecting it
Typically presents weeks after minor skin trauma as a papulonodular or verrucous lesion on the hand or finger that may ulcerate
Can spread proximally along lymphatics as a chain of nodules (sporotrichoid pattern), mimicking sporotrichosis
Deeper extension to tenosynovitis, septic arthritis, bursitis, or osteomyelitis occurs in a minority and often causes diagnostic delay
Diagnosis rests on biopsy for histology and mycobacterial culture, with the laboratory specifically asked to incubate at a lower temperature to recover the organism
Management is with macrolide-based combination antimicrobial therapy, often for several months, with surgical debridement reserved for deep or refractory infection
It carries the ESAT-6 and CFP-10 antigens and can therefore produce a positive interferon-gamma release assay, which should not be mistaken for tuberculosis
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium marinum is a ubiquitous inhabitant of fresh and salt water, including fish tanks and swimming pools. Infection follows inoculation of the organism through a break in the skin, usually on a hand or other distal site exposed during aquarium cleaning or fish handling. Because the bacterium grows optimally at temperatures below core body temperature, disease tends to remain localised to the cooler superficial tissues and rarely disseminates in immunocompetent people. A granulomatous inflammatory response develops at the inoculation site, producing the characteristic nodular or verrucous lesion, and organisms may track along lymphatic channels to produce ascending (sporotrichoid) nodules. In immunosuppressed hosts deeper and more extensive disease, including tenosynovitis and osteomyelitis, is more likely.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous tuberculosis (lupus vulgaris or tuberculosis verrucosa cutis)
Pyogenic granuloma or common viral wart
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy for histopathology demonstrating granulomatous inflammation
Mycobacterial culture of tissue with incubation at a lower temperature (around 30 degrees Celsius)
Acid-fast staining of tissue, recognising that yield is often low
Molecular identification (line-probe assay or gene sequencing) to speciate the isolate
Imaging (ultrasound or MRI) if deep structures such as tendon sheaths or bone are suspected
Assessment of immune status when disease is extensive or atypical
redFlags: Deep involvement with tenosynovitis, septic arthritis, or osteomyelitis requiring surgical input
Extensive or disseminated disease suggesting significant immunosuppression
Progressive lesions despite prolonged empirical antibacterial therapy
Functional impairment of the hand from tendon-sheath involvement
reference.prognosis: Localised cutaneous disease usually responds well to prolonged combination therapy with a good outcome, although resolution is slow. Deep infection of tendons, joints, or bone often requires surgery and may leave residual functional impairment, and treatment delay is common because the diagnosis is not initially suspected.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about aquarium, fish, or water exposure so the diagnosis is never considered
Not requesting culture at a lower incubation temperature, leading to falsely negative cultures
Mistaking sporotrichoid spread for fungal sporotrichosis and treating incorrectly
Interpreting a positive interferon-gamma release assay as tuberculosis
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
